questions.question: A ReadableStream with highWaterMark 2 has a pull() source and nobody has read from it yet. How many times is pull() called?
options: Zero — pull only runs after the first read
Twice — it stops once the internal queue reaches the high-water mark
questions.explanation: The stream calls pull only while its queue is below the high-water mark, so it fills to 2 chunks and then waits for a consumer to make room.

questions.question: What does `await writer.ready` do in a manual write loop?
options: Waits until the sink has room in its queue, applying backpressure to the producer
Waits until the whole stream is closed
Locks the stream so no other writer can use it
questions.explanation: writer.ready resolves when desiredSize is positive again, so awaiting it before each write keeps the producer from outrunning a slow sink.

questions.question: Why does the line-splitting transform keep a buffer and implement flush()?
options: Because TransformStream requires every transform to have flush()
To make the stream run in parallel
Because chunks can end mid-line, so the incomplete tail must be held and emitted when the input ends
questions.explanation: Chunk boundaries are arbitrary; the transform keeps the partial last piece and flush() emits whatever remains once the source closes.

questions.question: In Node, why is `pipeline()` from node:stream/promises preferred over chaining `.pipe()`?
options: pipeline is faster because it skips backpressure
pipeline forwards errors and destroys all the streams when one fails, while .pipe() does not
pipeline converts Node streams into Web Streams automatically
questions.explanation: .pipe() does not propagate errors or clean up the other streams, which can leak file handles; pipeline handles error propagation and cleanup and returns a promise.
